He claimed, in the 11th century, to have come up with deductive proof of God’s existence, through what we now know as the ontological argument. And, if there was such a thing as a social
network of medieval Christian philosophers back then, it was positively abuzz with the
news. For a long time. Because, almost 200 years later, Italian theologian and philosopher
Thomas Aquinas encountered Anselm’s argument. But, like many others, he just didn’t buy
it. Aquinas did believe in God. It was just that,
as a philosopher, he felt that it was important to have evidence for your beliefs. He knew
that if he was going to dismiss Anselm’s argument, he’d need to come up with something
better. So, he set out to construct five arguments that would prove God’s existence, once and
for all. Yeah, five. Apparently, he was concerned one
wasn’t going to do it, so he figured that, out of five, one was bound to stick. His first four arguments are known together
as the cosmological arguments, as they seek to prove God’s existence through what he
argued were necessary facts about the universe. So, in keeping with the method that we discussed
in our very first episode, we’re going to examine these first four arguments of Thomas
Aquinas -- and really try to understand them. And then we’ll consider their merits…
...and their weaknesses. [Theme Music] Maybe the most striking thing about the cosmological
arguments of Aquinas, at least to modern eyes, is that some of them are firmly based in the
natural world. Even though he lived in a pretty unscientific time, Aquinas argued for the
existence of God through his understanding of science, and with the help of what he thought
was physical evidence. For example, the first of his cosmological
arguments is known as the Argument from Motion. In it, Aquinas observed that we currently
live in a world in which things are moving. And he also observed that movement is caused
by movers -- things that cause motion. Aquinas was convinced that everything that’s moving
must have been set into motion by something else that was moving. By this logic, something
must have started the motion in the first place. Otherwise, you’d be stuck in a philosophical
quandary known as an infinite regress. You get an infinite regress when, in a chain of
reasoning, the evidence for each point along the chain relies on the existence of something
that came before it, which in turn relies on something even further back, and so on,
with no starting point. Basically, Aquinas thought the very idea of
infinite regress was absurd, logically impossible. Because, it implied that any given series
of events began with…nothing. Or, more accurately, never really began. Instead, it could have
been going on forever. In the case of physical motion, Aquinas wanted
to trace the cause of the movement he saw in the world all the way back to its beginning.

these blocks fall, and being told that nothing ever pushed over the first block. Instead,
they had always been falling down forever, backward into eternity. There must have been
a time when nothing was in motion, Aquinas thought, and there also must’ve been a static
being that started the motion. And that being, according to Aquinas, is God – the Unmoved
Mover. So his Argument From Motion ran something
like this: Objects are in motion
Everything in motion was put into motion by something else
There can’t be an infinite regress of movers So there must have been a first mover, itself
unmoved, and that is God Now, the second cosmological argument

going back in time. And we can’t have a world where everything is contingent, Aquinas

**Anselm of Canterbury and Thomas Aquinas: Arguments for God's Existence**

This transcript outlines the arguments used by 12th-century philosopher Thomas Aquinas to prove God’s existence, building on the work of his predecessor Anselm. 

**The Ontological Argument**: Anselm first presented his argument, proposing that God's existence could be demonstrated through a "necessary being."

**Arguments from Motion and Causation:** Aquinas built upon Anselm's ideas, developing four cosmological arguments. The "Argument from Motion" seeks to establish the necessity of a First Mover in nature; "Causal Necessity" focuses on the dependency relationships between cause and effect in the universe. 

**The Argument from Contingency:** Aquinas further explored the concept of necessary vs. contingent beings, asserting that there must exist something **necessary** to prevent infinite regress in contingency.


Let me know if you need more information about these arguments or a further breakdown!

The transcript discusses Thomas Aquinas' four cosmological arguments aimed at proving God's existence.

**Argument From Motion:** Aquinas argued that motion requires a mover and thus a first cause, concluding this force of creation must have been God (Unmoved Mover). The argument presented the idea of an infinite regress, which could be caused by an absurd lack of starting point for anything in the universe. As a solution, he proposed something with no prior causes, such as God, came before everything else. 

**Argument from Causation:** Similar to the first, this argued that cause and effect must exist within every interaction where you have things influencing each other. Because without a beginning, one wouldn't be able to trace back every event in the universe, Aquinas concluded there should be something causing all the events happening, which is ultimately God - the uncaused.  

**Argument from Contingency:** To avoid a regression that leads to nothing existing, Aquinas believed an uncaused being is essential. That reasoning involved contingent things and their potential to cause other contingent things; however, a continuous regress where nothing ever truly exists is impossible. This argument concludes there must be at least one necessary being – God – as the sole reason the entire world was created and exist.

**Argument with Measuring Sticks:** The last argument discussed the importance of comparison for measuring things like good or bad, or big and small by using other pre-established values to understand their relative size. This is about defining values in relation to other things so that they cannot exist as a standalone element.

In order to prove God's existence using natural facts about the universe, Thomas Aquinas proposed four cosmological arguments. This episode will examine these arguments and assess their merits and weaknesses.

Aquinas’ cosmological arguments are particularly striking because they grounded in the natural world. Despite living during a time marked by unscientific views, he argued for the existence of God through his understanding of science and physical evidence. For example, the Argument from Motion argues that we currently live in a moving world. Aquinas observed that movement occurs due to movers—objects that cause motion. Aquinas was convinced that everything in motion must have been set into motion by something else in motion. This reasoning means there has to have been a first mover, as otherwise,  you'd be stuck in an infinite regress, a chain of reason where evidence for each point in the line relies on the existence of something else that came before it; a non-ending process with no starting point. The very idea of an infinite regress is philosophically absurd because it implies that any given series of events began with nothing or never really began as if things just "always" existed. Aquinas thought that tracing the cause of movement in the world back to its beginning was crucial in seeing there had to have been a first mover, God. If not for this, watching objects fall would be like a scene where nothing ever pushed over the first block - their motion would just go on forever. 

Aquinas believed there must of existed a time when things were still; and he further proposed an idea that is the Unmoved Mover—God. His Argument from Motion ran something along these lines: Objects are in motion
Everything in motion was put into motion by something else
There can’t be an infinite regress of movers 
So there must have been a First mover, itself unmoved, and that is God

Similarly to the first argument, the second cosmological argument – the Argument from Causation - aimed at avoiding the problem of an infinite regress. By explaining causation, instead of explaining motion, it addressed cause-and-effect in a grander scale across the entire universe. This followed these lines: Some things are caused
Anything that’s caused has to be caused
by something else (since nothing causes itself) 
There can’t be an infinite regress of causes
So there must have been a first causer, itself uncaused, and that is God

As with the Argument from Motion, Aquinas' reasoning here was straightforward: effects must always have their cause, and to avoid an infinite regress. Think about how you ended up watching a video like this—we can trace a chain of causation going backward, almost forever in this instance. You might see further back than it seems as long as the process has been observed. However, Aquinas said this couldn't happen "forever." There had to be something that started off everything we know today and we've all witnessed how change works! For a good point; let’s say you are lucky enough to exist - to look back from where you stand right now-  There’s a good chance your existence is contingent upon some other things being present. You exist because sperm met an egg, swapped genes, and we don't really have that much control! But what does that tell us about God? Aquinas thought it was important to consider that in order for there to be an infinite regress of contingency, something had to prevent these kinds of movements from going on forever, something to keep these things from turning into nothing.  He needed at least one necessary being – a being that has always existed, always will exist and cannot not be, in order to make the whole "thing" grow. This necessary being is God.

Motion and Causation:  Saint Thomas Aquinas developed four cosmological arguments to demonstrate the existence of God.  These arguments focused on explaining the concept of cause and effect in the universe. 

Argument From Motion: 
Aquinas established a chain of causes for everything in motion, arguing that unless there was an initial force or "First Mover," it would be like watching blocks fall forever; nothing started it. He claimed God is this Unmoved Mover as the beginning source of all motion.  

Second Argument: Argument From Causation
This argument applied to causation in general, claiming that every cause necessitates another until finding a First Causer. Aquinas positing God as this Uncaused Causer. 

Argument From Contingency:
The argument from contingency focused on non-existent beings and how an infinite regress of contingency undermines the natural order of existence. 

To illustrate, he argues, “Something’s Contingent” is not possible; everything requires a necessary being; and hence comes the necessity of God.  


 Argument From Degrees: 
Aquinas concluded by showing that every thing’s value must have a basis point of reference to define its relative worth; this reference is God, as defined perfectly, perfect in essence- “The Pinnacle of Perfection.” This argument for God's existence is based on the inherent value and order established through degrees – like grade point percentages. 
  


It is important to note that while Aquinas developed clear reasoning around these arguments to demonstrate the presence of God from natural and philosophical principles; many philosophers since then have found issues with them, leaving room for a continued debate in philosophy and theology, despite their significant contributions to the understanding of divine creation..

There was a general belief that objects must begin by moving from something else. This reasoning suggests there must be a starting point for motion and is called an infinite regress. An infinite regress is established when, in a line of reasoning, one argument relies on an existing event that depends on another; with no beginning to this series. Thomas Aquinas believed the idea of an infinite regress was absurd, or impossible, due to it implied something started without origin. Instead, he suggested if you look at physical motion, something must've been responsible for initiating movement in this world, and there must have been a first-mover for example. Aquinas also argued that God's existence could be confirmed by the concept of an unmoved mover being the cause of all motion. 

Thomas Aquinas developed three cosmological arguments: First, he focused on motion starting from nothing to demonstrate something began everything. Second, the argument used the connection between causation and effects, showing that one can't exist without its effect until other objects are present. Third, his argument centered on contingency - a being with existence determined to be necessary as anything else could not have existed; and thus must have been created by God. 

Aquinas developed his last point through an argument that things exist because of the contingent nature in which they are dependent upon one another. The world can't exist without some kind of anchor – for an example, like God is a perfect being that serves as a standard for creation, meaning all other items are measured in relation to what it implies. 


This was Thomas Aquinas's reasoning, known as the Argument from Degrees. Properties come in degrees and perfection cannot be present by itself; something would always be superior to it. So ultimately, Aquinas came to believe that God must be perfect- a reference point across the entire universe of things.

Despite this reasoning, Aquinas's arguments remain a controversial subject, leaving most philosophers unimpressed or skeptical of their argumentative power; they're not able to establish God's existence based on these four arguments alone; but even when you'd expect them to do so!

Aquinas' Cosmological Arguments for the Existence of God

Aquinas presented four cosmological arguments supporting the existence of God: **1. The Argument from Motion:** - Objects in motion were caused by other objects, leading to an infinite regress problem. - Aquinas proposed that there had to be a first mover, an unmoved and unchanging entity – this is God. **2. The Argument from Causation:** - Everything has a cause except for a thing itself; this chain of causes was necessary in the universe. - Thus, things ultimately had a cause that was not without causation (God). **3. The Argument from Contingency:** - Contingent beings are those that might not exist and include all beings; nothing can be born or killed except through God. - Aquinas believed in one necessary being for contingency, which is God. **4. The Argument From Degrees of Perfection (Argument from Degrees):** - Properties and concepts like 'good' come with degrees - that means there must be a perfect entity against which all else is measured. - This perfection is identified by the ultimate being (god). ## Criticisms While Aquinas’ arguments presented an intriguing approach to demonstrating God’s existence, they have encountered challenges. For starters, these cosmological arguments are not able to definitively establish the existence of a Christian god, nor do they directly address theological concepts like omnibenevolence or feelings. This criticism is often seen as highlighting a lack of personal or emotional connection between Aquinas' god and how people usually approach God in their prayer rituals and prayers for help. Another key point is that these arguments fail to exclude the notion of polytheistic ideas, leaving the door open for the existence of multiple deities (multiple gods) as the solution for his conclusions. Ultimately, philosophers continue to dissect and analyze the validity and limitations of Aquinas’ arguments despite their significant contributions.

Philosopher Thomas Aquinas proposed four cosmological arguments aiming to prove the existence of God. The arguments center around several core concepts:

**Argument 1: First Cause:**  Aquinas claimed there is an initial "First Thing" that sparked a chain of events. This first thing, he stated unequivocally, must be God because it provides necessary order and prevents an infinite regress of cause-and-effect where everything relies on its preceding instance, potentially leading to the non-existence of anything.

**Argument 2: Contingency:** Aquinas argued for the necessity of God due to the inherent possibility of contingent things—objects, properties, events, etc., that *could* not have existed (including humanity). This necessitates a necessary Being, God, who acts as a grounding concept against the endless potential of existence itself.

**Argument 3: Measuring Stick:** This argument posited that we use concrete measurements of the good, bad, large, and small for value comparison. It hinges on applying absolute measurement to contingent things like human achievement. Aquinas proposes that there must be something inherently perfect beyond which all others must be measured—God.  

**Argument 4: Degrees:** This argument suggests a hierarchy exists within these established parameters (e.g., size, value, etc.), and thus a perfect "point of reference" is required for comparison. For Aquinas, the existence of an eternally perfect God (God being in its own right the ultimate point of reference used) becomes this necessary ideal for all else to be relative against

**Challenges & Criticisms**:

* **Infinite Regress:** The idea that every cause must have a cause prior remains contested. Critics believe it's implausible without contradicting itself and further implying an external force (God). 
*  **Flaw of Arguments:** Some argue that Aquinas' own arguments for God’s existence are not inherently robust. It weakens these arguments when their foundation is called into question; the reasoning becomes faulty, as if its conclusion must be invalidated for it to stand true in terms of reason itself. The use of logic and argument needs more than simply affirming a conclusion; otherwise, conclusions don't stand up to scrutiny.  
* **Self-Defeating:** A counterargument by critics was made regarding the arguments’ reliance on "necessity." If God is subject to causes like others, then His role in existence as the ultimate cause isn't necessarily true. This undermines the argument for God being the necessary starting point.




In sum, while Aquinas' cosmological arguments offer compelling insights into the nature of order in the universe and our existential needs, their strength and validity face critique from numerous points; leading to ongoing discussions about divine attributes and the potential limitations of reasoning itself when attempting to define the ultimate "first cause" as a singular concept capable of containing all things.

### Aquinas' Cosmological Arguments Explained

Philosophers have long debated the existence of God, and Thomas Aquinas developed four cosmological arguments to support this claim. 

**Aquinas' Key Premises:**
* **Existence Necessity:** Everything existing inherently necessitates a higher power – God. This is the beginning point for understanding everything.
* **Measuring Value:**  A basis for evaluating value in something must exist as "something" itself. The value of things, like 'big/small', 'good/bad' exist within a scale and comparison to another defined thing; this means there must be a "standard," some being of perfection – God.
 

**Argument from Degrees:** Aquinas believed that the existence of degrees defines something as existing, for example, in heat. For every degree there must exist something perfect, it's the highest point - This being, God.


 **Critiques &  Limits to Aquinas' Arguments:**
* **Infinite Regress**:   The philosophy challenge questions if there can be an infinite regress of contingent things, and if that’s even possible, does God have to exist? 
* **Self-Defeating Argument**:  If everything must have a cause because its a being, doesn’t that mean God could also require a reason for his own existence. 


**Alternative Philosophies:** 
Some believe Aquinas' cosmological argument is flawed because it only shows God as an absolute being and not necessarily emotionally engaged. The idea that multiple Gods may exist is introduced; their argument challenges Aquinas' conclusion with counter-arguments to support their own view of the ultimate cause.  

**Conclusion of Philosophical Inquiry**:


The arguments presented serve as a beginning point for philosophical discussions:  
 1) **Accepting an Argument’s Conclusion:** Whether the argument is strong or weak, accepting it as true can exist without necessarily confirming the final conclusion, particularly on God's existence.
2.) **Counter Arguments:** One must offer counterpoints to an argument that they do not agree with and find what their belief's validity truly is. 


Overall, Aquinas’ philosophical arguments are complex; however his approach to establishing the necessity of God has created a lasting contribution to philosophical debate about God’s existence today.

### Summary of Aquinas' Cosmological Arguments  

This transcript discusses Thomas Aquinas' four cosmological arguments for the existence of God. 

**Aquinas' Argument Structure:** 

1. **Existence Defined by Perfection:** Aquinas argued that if there were no anchor to define value, everything in space would be floating randomly with no meaningful relationship. He concluded that God was this "anchor" element defining all values, and His perfection serves as a benchmark for everything else.

2. **Challenges to the Argument:** These arguments have faced criticism for not definitively establishing the existence of a particular god. Many philosophers, even bothists and atheists, find these arguments unsatisfying. 

**Philosophical Objections:**

* The argument's limitations: Aquinas' cosmological proofs didn't establish God as we perceive him (who feels and cares). Instead, his reasoning presented "unmoved movers" (god that operates in a way outside of our world), and "uncaused causer."


 **Multiple Gods &  Self-Defeating Arguments**

* Polytheism: Aquinas’ arguments do not eliminate the possibility of multiple gods. They leave room for a polytheistic approach to God's existence. This objection also calls into question infinite regress; Aquinas argued for a defined starting point, but some argue that this assumption can be false. 
* Self-Defeating: the argument itself presents problems: if everything must have a cause, then even potentially god must have a causal chain. Therefore, Aquinas could prove god is subject to the same logical chains as other things, weakening his arguments.

 **Philosophy and Dialogue:** 

Even though Aquinas’ philosophical work has been challenging over centuries (due to its inherent self-contradiction), he started a debate about God which continues to this date with philosophers engaging with these arguments and forming their own counter-arguments. This makes philosophy valuable and requires continual growth in the face of challenges, especially after hundreds of years.
